results.verified_title: China’s cooling-equipment industrial capacity and its implications for European climate adaptation
results.source_identity_basis: Opened ECFR commentary by Byford Tsang, Senior Policy Fellow, dated 18 August 2026, matching the exact assigned headline and URL. It is a policy commentary supported with cited data, not an experimental paper or primary manufacturer audit.
results.source_type: Independent think-tank policy analysis / structural technology-market evidence
results.evidence_location: ECFR sections “China leads on AC,” “Saying no to adaptation,” and “What Europeans should do”; International Energy Agency (IEA), 10 July 2026, sections “More air conditioners are being sold” and Chinese manufacturing capacity.
results.specific_finding: China’s large-scale cooling-equipment manufacturing and supply chains are a strategically relevant technological capability for adaptation to rising heat demand: IEA estimates roughly 170 million Chinese AC units manufactured and 60 million exported per year, while ECFR documents the resulting European sourcing dependencies and Chinese firms’ product localisation.
results.primary_evidence_summary: ECFR examines Chinese air-conditioner industry specialisation, adaptation to European installation constraints, energy-efficient refrigerants, public procurement, technology transfer and the risks of relying on a single clean-tech supply chain. IEA independently estimates Chinese manufacturing and export scale and describes cooling efficiency standards and growing electricity demand.
results.corroboration_assessment: IEA is a separate international analytical institution and provides quantitative manufacturing/export scale and global cooling-demand evidence. Its analysis corroborates structural exposure, not all ECFR forecasts, trade-share percentages or policy prescriptions.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Cooling is becoming essential energy infrastructure; supply concentration shapes access to efficient appliances, adaptation technology, product standards and research-to-manufacturing scale-up. European resilience depends on efficiency innovation, diversified supply chains and careful technology-transfer choices.
results.eu_radar_comparison: The exact ECFR commentary is already in the main Radar. This verification extends it with IEA’s independent manufacturing and electricity-demand data, and reframes it as structural innovation and industrial capability rather than evidence of a new laboratory breakthrough.
results.method_and_limitations: ECFR is an opinionated strategic interpretation; it does not measure Chinese R&D quality or prove policy causality. IEA numbers are rounded estimates for manufacturing and markets, not a quality audit. China-specific AC export percentages in ECFR were not separately verified here.
results.reviewer_notes: Evidence supports a cooling-industry/technology-capacity finding, NOT an independent new climate-science discovery. Avoid repeating ECFR’s quoted EU-China trade percentages as verified without original data.

results.verified_title: UNESCO UIS 2026 R&D data release — Russia-specific finding not established
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: The assigned UNESCO Institute for Statistics release exists and was opened, but it provides global and regional indicators rather than a Russia-specific multi-year R&D funding or researcher series. HSE’s 2026 Russian data book and 2024 national figures are possible leads, not independent confirmation that the UIS release establishes a Russian trend.
results.reviewer_notes: UIS reports global R&D intensity rising from 1.71% of GDP (2015) to 1.92% (2023) and researchers per million from 1,141 to 1,486; these are global aggregates, not Russia values. HSE Russian official statistics include nominal and real year-to-year figures, but cross-dataset definitions and source independence need a Russia time-series comparison. The same UNESCO release was already unresolved in the previous reviewed batch.

results.verified_title: US federal R&D obligations flattened in FY2025 as defence priorities expanded
results.source_identity_basis: Opened US National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES), Survey of Federal Funds for Research and Development, FYs 2024–2025 (Volume 74), released 4 May 2026. The exact named survey, years, official publisher and FY2025 provisional status match the assignment.
results.source_type: US official federal R&D census and statistics
results.evidence_location: NCSES Data Highlights and 4 May 2026 Featured Survey Analysis NSF 26-317; federal obligation tables for FY2024 and FY2025; OECD 31 March 2026 R&D statistical release, government R&D budget section.
results.specific_finding: US federal agency R&D obligations rose from $186.1 billion in FY2023 to $194.2 billion in FY2024 (+4.4% nominal), but preliminary FY2025 obligations were $194.1 billion (−0.1% nominal and approximately −2.3% inflation-adjusted). Defence R&D obligations increased by about $12.3 billion from FY2023 to FY2024 as research-budget composition shifted.
results.primary_evidence_summary: NCSES annual agency census reports FY2024 DOD R&D obligations of approximately $97.9 billion and preliminary FY2025 around $93.4 billion. It describes a shrinking HHS component after COVID-era funding. The distinction between obligations and appropriations is explicit; FY2025 numbers are preliminary.
results.corroboration_assessment: OECD provides a different cross-country budget-allocation series, reporting 2025 US government budget allocations for R&D fell 7.9% in real terms among available comparable reporting countries. This independently supports tightening public budgets, but the OECD budget series is NOT the same measure as NCSES obligations.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Changes in funding composition affect US universities, early-career researchers, federal laboratories and transatlantic scientific partnerships. Priority shifts towards security and defence may alter research opportunities and availability of openly collaborative work.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact main Radar record for the 2024–25 NCSES survey was identified in the package. This adds verified US funding and defence-prioritisation evidence to an EU-centred discussion; other topical Radar coverage is possible.
results.method_and_limitations: FY2025 values are provisional agency estimates; obligations differ from approved budgets and actual expenditures. Nominal and real comparisons cannot be merged. OECD and NCSES definitions differ; a subsequent fiscal settlement can revise the trend.

results.verified_title: United Kingdom funds early-career research at the security–fundamental-science interface
results.source_identity_basis: Opened dated UK Research and Innovation news release “UKRI-backed fellowships support emerging research talent,” 21 October 2026. It directly identifies the UKRI-backed Intelligence Community Postdoctoral Research Fellowships and awardees; separately checked the delivery academy’s awardee announcement.
results.source_type: UK public research-funder award announcement / talent programme
results.evidence_location: UKRI 21 October 2026 release: 11 fellowships, 24-person Royal Academy of Engineering wider cohort, topic list and Industrial Strategy National Security and Defence link; Royal Academy of Engineering joint research/ICRF awardee announcement, UK IC fellowship notes.
results.specific_finding: UKRI backed 11 UK Intelligence Community postdoctoral fellowships in 2026 within a wider 24-person early-career researcher announcement. The scheme funds unclassified fundamental research relevant to security, defence, AI, quantum sensing and communications, with government-linked technical mentoring and end-user connections.
results.primary_evidence_summary: UKRI explicitly names the 11 awards and examples including detection of synthetic audio; the Royal Academy of Engineering independently publishes the awardee cohort and documents that the IC postdoctoral fellowships offer up to £250,000 over two years to support unclassified fundamental research.
results.corroboration_assessment: Royal Academy of Engineering is the fellowship delivery body on another domain and confirms awardees and scheme structure. This is strong independent-publisher confirmation of an administrative decision, but not independent evaluation of later research results.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: The programme illustrates a UK institutional method for aligning early-career research capacity with security-relevant long-term challenges without classifying the funded fundamental research. It can matter to European research-talent policy and science–security partnerships.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact main Radar match was identified for these UKRI 2026 fellowships. Distinct from the earlier verified UK innovation-ranking and university spin-out findings: this one concerns targeted research talent and mission-linked fellowships.
results.method_and_limitations: Awards and programme design are documented, not achievements in research output, national security or commercialisation. Fellowship ceilings are maximum grant values; cohort sizes and programme components must not be conflated.

results.verified_title: FAPESP Week highlights Brazil–Netherlands science cooperation
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: The assigned 30 October FAPESP story and a related FAPESP agency report credibly describe the Netherlands symposium, reported bilateral amendment, and a claim of over 1,000 São Paulo–Netherlands joint publications per year. However, I did not independently verify the newly signed agreement or the bibliometric claim from a Dutch institutional publication or underlying publication dataset; the event programme is issued by FAPESP itself.
results.reviewer_notes: Good structural lead: the reported model includes 10-year centres, international research centres and bilateral calls. The official Brazilian travel-authorisation record corroborates attendance at FAPESP Week but not the agreement or claimed joint-paper count. Revisit if NWO releases the signed amendment or independently comparable co-publication data become available.

results.verified_title: NRF-SAASTA amplifies health research through digital media
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: The 2 October 2026 NRF-SAASTA article primarily reports photographing, filming and livestreaming a local health-research conference. It does not establish a substantive new biomedical research result, healthcare innovation capability, funding change or evidence-based trend; publicity reach is not evidence of research impact.
results.reviewer_notes: The conference may be useful as a contact or source-discovery lead, but the specific assigned article fails the threshold for a verified international health or biotechnology R&I finding. Original NRF page timed out on direct access; its indexed published article text was available.

results.verified_title: India converts selected innovation capabilities into outputs despite constrained R&D intensity
results.source_identity_basis: Opened WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 official entry page and full GII 2026 results text released 29 September 2026. Checked the India economy profile/ranking results against the assigned country, and examined India’s official Economic Survey 2025–26 for separate investment-context evidence.
results.source_type: Intergovernmental composite innovation benchmark with national economic context
results.evidence_location: WIPO 2026 GII Results: middle-income economies and innovation-input/output performance; India country profile (2026 input rank 49, output rank 25); India Economic Survey 2025–26 sections 8.48–8.49 on gross R&D expenditure and business contribution.
results.specific_finding: India ranked 38th in the Global Innovation Index 2026, with innovation outputs 25th versus inputs 49th. WIPO describes sustained long-term innovation gains and an unusually strong position in ICT services exports. India’s Economic Survey independently reports R&D spending around 0.64% of GDP and a business-sector share around 41%, indicating that select high-performing output domains coexist with a relatively thin R&D resource base.
results.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO ranks India in the top 40 and as the leading economy in its income and regional groups; its output rank is much stronger than its input rank. India’s Economic Survey 2025–26 attributes low R&D spending intensity in part to the small private-sector contribution and details new RDI and research-foundation instruments aimed at raising capacity.
results.corroboration_assessment: The Indian Economic Survey provides separately produced national R&D spending and institutional-policy evidence, not an independent re-ranking of WIPO scores. The Government of India document corroborates constraints and the policy response, while WIPO supplies the international comparative index.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: India is an instructive case of the separation between aggregate research investment and specialised innovation outputs. European R&I comparisons should examine digital services, commercial linkages and innovation-finance mechanisms rather than assuming spending rank equals output rank.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact main Radar India 2026 GII entry was identified. This adds a structural input-output pattern and national funding context, not a claim that India exceeds EU economies in aggregate R&D performance.
results.method_and_limitations: GII rankings are composites and ordinal positions, not causal productivity measures. Indicators have different reference years (mostly 2024–26); the Indian Economic Survey’s R&D intensity series is older than GII publication and uses national definitions. Changes in rank also reflect changes in other countries.

results.verified_title: Australia returns to the global innovation top 20 as research links and business R&D strengthen
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the WIPO Global Innovation Index 2026 official homepage and full 2026 results; WIPO explicitly discusses Australia returning to rank 20 with its 2026 input/output balance. Checked the separate Australian Bureau of Statistics business R&D survey released in August 2025 and Australia parliamentary research context.
results.source_type: Intergovernmental innovation-index series with official domestic R&D statistics
results.evidence_location: WIPO 2026 GII results section “Australia, Canada and New Zealand regain ground”; Australian Bureau of Statistics “Research and Experimental Development, Businesses, Australia, 2023–24” key statistics and annual expenditure comparison.
results.specific_finding: Australia rose to 20th in WIPO’s 2026 innovation index (from 22nd in 2025), with inputs ranked 13th but outputs 24th. WIPO cites stronger university–industry collaboration and clusters; separately, Australia’s statistics bureau reports business R&D expenditure of A$24.41 billion in 2023–24, up 18% from 2021–22 in current prices.
results.primary_evidence_summary: WIPO reports a partial recovery in Australian innovation ranking and identifies world-class universities and university–industry R&D collaboration among its strengths. ABS shows a measurable increase in business R&D expenditure over two financial years, alongside an expanded R&D workforce; rankings and investment data are separate kinds of evidence.
results.corroboration_assessment: ABS is a different institution and domain and corroborates the business R&D input trend using national survey data. Parliament’s earlier research review provides independent context on Australia’s historical gap between innovation inputs and outputs; neither independently reconstructs WIPO’s composite 2026 rank.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Australia combines strong universities with a longstanding challenge in translation to outputs. Its renewed R&D spending and collaboration infrastructure are relevant comparators for EU industry–university knowledge transfer and innovation-system benchmarking.
results.eu_radar_comparison: No exact main Radar match for this 2026 Australia GII assessment was identified. It adds an Oceania structural comparison to an otherwise EU-centred picture.
results.method_and_limitations: GII year-to-year ranking changes can reflect methodology and other economies; the ABS 2023–24 expenditure data predate the 2026 index and are nominal, not proof of innovation outputs. A 2026 rank is a composite benchmark, not an observed causal result.

results.verified_title: Vietnam and EU establish a more structured science and innovation cooperation channel
results.source_identity_basis: Opened the Austrian ERA Portal’s 27 May 2026 note “EU and Vietnam deepen cooperation in science, technology and innovation,” which matches the assigned URL and title. Separately checked the European Commission’s actual 27 May signing statement and Vietnam Ministry of Science and Technology reporting on 28 May.
results.source_type: Research-policy cooperation announcement, corroborated by two parties
results.evidence_location: ERA Portal: agreement on joint research and mobility, Horizon Europe participation; European Commission DG RTD 27 May 2026 news release on signed Letter of Intent; Vietnam Ministry of Science and Technology 28 May report on cooperative mechanism and research institutions.
results.specific_finding: The European Commission and Vietnam’s Ministry of Science and Technology signed a Letter of Intent on 27 May 2026 to increase research, researcher-mobility, technology-transfer and university–industry cooperation. The Commission reports 32 Vietnamese participations in 29 signed Horizon Europe grants, giving a concrete baseline for wider scientific integration.
results.primary_evidence_summary: Austrian ERA Portal reports a new EU–Vietnam research cooperation framework; the Commission specifies the signed Letter of Intent in Hanoi and its target areas of AI, digital and green technologies. Vietnam’s science ministry describes the parallel national perspective on increasing research participation and advanced technology transfer.
results.corroboration_assessment: The European Commission and Vietnam Ministry of Science and Technology directly confirm the bilateral administrative decision on separate domains. Both are parties to the agreement, so this validates the signed intent but not later increases in research mobility, funded grants or commercial results.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: Vietnam is growing as an international collaborator and research-innovation partner, suggesting a more reciprocal model for European engagement with Southeast Asian talent, universities and firms. Horizon participation provides an initial observable baseline.
results.eu_radar_comparison: The precise ERA Portal summary is already in the main Radar. This confirms it independently with statements from the signatories and adds the grant-participation baseline; it does not claim a previously unseen event.
results.method_and_limitations: A Letter of Intent is a commitment to seek cooperation, not a funded programme or realised exchange. The 32 participations/29 grants are baseline totals reported by the EU and not causal outcomes of the 2026 letter. Both signatories have promotional incentives.

results.verified_title: China’s electric-vehicle industry exemplifies investment-led technological scaling under dual circulation
results.source_identity_basis: Opened full open-access research article in Asia Europe Journal, Springer Nature, published 26 August 2026, by Miguel Otero-Iglesias, Federico Steinberg and Agustín González-Agote. The publication’s exact title and DOI match the assigned https://doi.org/10.1007/s10308-026-00785-0 redirect.
results.source_type: Peer-reviewed/open-access political economy study with external sector statistics
results.evidence_location: Asia Europe Journal abstract, introduction, “State of play” and “Impact on Europe” sections; IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 executive summary and “Manufacturing and trade” chapters, covering 2025 Chinese output, exports and battery production.
results.specific_finding: The study argues China’s dual-circulation approach reinforces industrial scaling and control of strategic inputs despite weak domestic consumption. Independent IEA 2026 data show China manufactured nearly 75% of electric cars globally in 2025, accounted for over 80% of battery-cell production, and more than doubled EV exports to over 2.5 million, demonstrating the scale of the industrial-technology ecosystem.
results.primary_evidence_summary: The article draws on a literature review and workshop/interview insights to interpret state-led industrial upgrading, electric vehicle competitiveness and Europe’s vulnerability. IEA’s measured manufacturing and trade data confirm enormous Chinese EV/battery scale, but do not establish a single-cause link between the dual-circulation policy and this outcome.
results.corroboration_assessment: IEA’s independently assembled international sales and manufacturing series corroborate the sector’s massive scale and 2025 export expansion. They do not independently validate the authors’ political-economy causal interpretation, which remains an analytic argument.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: A strategy of scaling production capacity, embedded supply chains, battery inputs and indigenous innovation can turn research capabilities into globally competitive systems. EU industrial policy should distinguish research inventions, process learning, integration and supply chain control.
results.eu_radar_comparison: The exact DOI is already present in the main Radar; this review confirms the real peer-reviewed work, adds IEA market evidence and explicitly separates empirical manufacturing scale from causal interpretation.
results.method_and_limitations: The paper primarily synthesises literature and stakeholder interviews rather than causal experiments. The authors’ claim that domestic weakness drives external advantage is contestable; IEA volume figures do not identify causality. Production share is not equivalent to research quality or innovation originality.

results.verified_title: ALLEA contributes to high-level discussions on science in Ukraine’s recovery
results.reason_for_review_or_drop: The assigned 27 June 2026 ALLEA article and July 2026 European Commission account accurately document the Gdańsk Declaration and the shift toward longer-term Ukrainian research-system recovery. But this is substantively the same research-capacity recovery signal already accepted into the previous Global Deep Scan batch; importing it again would create a duplicate verified finding.
results.reviewer_notes: Not a rejection of Ukraine or the credibility of ALLEA. The source is already in the main Radar, and the previous KEEP was “Ukraine research support evolves from emergency grants toward durable collaboration and research-system rebuilding.” New goals such as the conditional 3%-of-GDP aspiration can be noted in that existing finding rather than creating a separate redundant record.

results.verified_title: US total R&D growth diverges from contracting government research budgets in 2024–25
results.source_identity_basis: Opened OECD Main Science and Technology Indicators dataset landing page, which explicitly provides the March 2026 release cycle and links to its 31 March 2026 statistical briefing. The assigned page is a regularly updated dataset, so 31 March 2026 refers to the dated companion analytical release, not an invented publication date for the landing page.
results.source_type: Intergovernmental cross-country R&D series and dated statistical briefing
results.evidence_location: OECD MSTI “MSTI release cycle and highlights”; OECD 31 March 2026 briefing, sections on 2024 total R&D growth and government budget allocations; US NCSES FY2024–25 survey federal R&D obligations section.
results.specific_finding: The OECD reports US inflation-adjusted total R&D spending grew 3.4% in 2024, much faster than the EU’s 0.4%, but government budget allocations for R&D were tightening; OECD reports a 7.9% real reduction in US 2025 government R&D allocations among the comparable countries then reporting. Private and government R&D trajectories therefore should not be conflated.
results.primary_evidence_summary: OECD MSTI series combines cross-country spending, personnel and budget indicators; its 31 March 2026 report distinguishes total national R&D expenditures from public research budget allocations. The US NCSES reports preliminary FY2025 federal obligations almost flat nominally and down in real terms, consistent with a tighter public pipeline despite the stronger all-sector spending base.
results.corroboration_assessment: NCSES is a different publishing institution and domain, supporting the direction of the federal public R&D slowdown using a distinct obligations measure; it does not independently calculate the OECD all-sector growth rate. Some OECD country inputs originate from national survey data, an important independence limit.
results.mechanism_and_ri_importance: The divergence between growing aggregate research expenditure and weakening public budgets can affect basic research, public infrastructure and universities even in innovation-leading countries. It invites careful US–EU comparison of funding composition and scientific workforce resilience, beyond league-table spending totals.
results.eu_radar_comparison: The OECD dataset was not an exact main Radar match in the assigned package. Unlike the FY2024–25 NCSES item in this same package, this finding concerns the contrast between economy-wide R&D growth and the government funding stream, not the absolute size of federal obligations.
results.method_and_limitations: The 2024 total-R&D growth and 2025 GBARD refer to different years, sectors and accounting definitions; they cannot be subtracted or interpreted as a single causal trajectory. OECD 2025 GBARD estimates include few reporting countries and remain subject to revision.
